_note: BE Mastery V2 — competency missions. The `week` of a competency is the General English programme week it teaches (weeks.json), NOT the order these were built: Week 1 'Explain what you do' — 5 moves; Week 2 'Give a clear update' — 4 moves; Week 3 'Raise a problem' — 5 moves; Week 4 'Clarifying, asking questions & confirming' — 4 moves (flag → ask → restate → confirm), no shadow block after a content check (see its _shadow_note). The first two were prototyped as 2 and 3 and were renumbered once the third arrived; `week` is display, analytics and the pickNext tie-break only — every store, route and record is keyed by competency id, so nothing had to be migrated. OPTIONAL curriculum section, General English only. A track without its own missions.json gets null, NOT the parent's: professional-tracks.js lists 'missions' in NEVER_INHERIT precisely so this content can never reach Welding through the curriculum merge. Content is written in English like every other pack (weeks.json, phrases.json); only the surrounding chrome is translated through t().

competencies.title: Explain what you do
competencies.objective: Explain your role and your current work so that someone who has never met your team understands it.
competencies.pattern: ROLE → RESPONSIBILITY → RIGHT NOW → WHO IT'S FOR → WHY IT MATTERS
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block on purpose. The 301-clip General English library has nothing about describing your own role — the nearest match is about expressing opinions — and inventing a link would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. The NOTICE step simply omits the Shadow row, and fromShadow() never links a clip to a competency that names none. Add a "shadow" block here the day a fitting clip exists.

moves.label: Role
moves.hint: What you are and where you sit. Name it in one short sentence.
patterns: I work as a logistics analyst.
My role sits between operations and finance.
I'm the person who looks after the supplier data.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by naming your job and the team you sit in.

moves.label: Responsibility
moves.hint: What is actually yours — the part that would go wrong without you.
patterns: I'm responsible for the weekly reports.
A big part of my role is checking supplier data.
I look after everything that leaves the warehouse.
moves.retry: Say it again and name one thing you are responsible for — the part that is yours.
cues: a big part of my role

moves.label: Right now
moves.hint: What is on your desk this week, not what you did last year.
patterns: At the moment I'm rebuilding the tracking sheet.
This week I'm focused on the supplier audit.
Right now we're moving everything onto the new system.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what you are working on at the moment.

moves.label: Who it's for
moves.hint: Who you work with, or who receives what you produce.
patterns: I work closely with the warehouse managers.
It goes to the finance team every Monday.
My main users are the people on the shop floor.
moves.retry: Say it again and say who you work with, or who your work is for.

moves.label: Why it matters
moves.hint: What it is for. The result, not the task.
patterns: …so the team can see a problem before the customer does.
It means nothing leaves the site unchecked.
The point is that nobody has to chase it by hand.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with what your work is actually for — what it makes possible.

expressions.def: the plain way to open with your job title

expressions.w: my role sits at the intersection of
expressions.def: for a job that spans two teams
names what you own

expressions.w: a big part of my role is
expressions.def: introduces your main responsibility
what is on your desk at the moment
names the people you depend on
learn what you need to know about something new
in agreement, sharing the same understanding

see.where: It is your first week. You are at lunch with someone from another department.
see.asks: So what do you actually do here?
see.goal: Answer in about 30 seconds so that someone outside your team understands your job and why it exists.

hear.model: I work as an operations analyst in the logistics team. I'm responsible for the weekly delivery reports and the supplier data. At the moment I'm rebuilding how we track late shipments. I work closely with the warehouse managers, so the team can see a problem before it reaches the customer.
hear.note: Five short sentences. One move each. No job title jargon.

missions.prompt: So what do you actually do here?
missions.context: They do not know your team, your tools or your acronyms. Assume they know nothing about your work except that it happens in this building.

see.where: A video call is starting with a client who has never met your team.
see.asks: Before we start — can you tell us a bit about your role?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time, and this is a first impression with someone outside the company.

missions.prompt: Before we start — can you tell us a bit about your role?
missions.context: They are paying for the work. They want to know who they are talking to and why you are the right person to be on this call.

competencies.title: Give a clear update
competencies.objective: Give a concise professional project update that a busy colleague can act on.

shadow.title: How to Organize Your Thoughts When Speaking English (Stop Rambling)
shadow.why: The same four-part shape, spoken at natural pace by a professional speaker.

moves.label: Status
moves.hint: Where the work actually is right now.
patterns: The project is on track.
We've completed the first two stages.
So far, everything is going to plan.
moves.retry: Give the update again and open with one clear sentence saying where the work is right now.
moves._cue_note: Phrase cues, not bare words. A single cue like "ready" or "done" would fire inside a next-step sentence ("we'll be ready tomorrow") and credit a status the learner never gave. Under-crediting is the safe direction here: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed, and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner only a retry.

moves.label: Issue
moves.hint: The one thing that is not going to plan.
patterns: We've run into a supplier issue.
We're held up waiting for approval.
The problem is a delay at the supplier.
moves.retry: Give the update again and name the one problem clearly, in a single sentence.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it means for the deadline, the cost or the customer. This is the move most people skip.
patterns: This may affect Friday's delivery.
It puts the deadline at risk.
That means we'd be two days late.
moves.retry: Give the update again and say clearly what the delay means for the deadline — name the date or the number of days.

moves.label: Next step
moves.hint: What you are doing about it, and when you will report back.
patterns: We're working with the supplier.
I'll have an update for you tomorrow.
The next step is to confirm a new date.
moves.retry: Give the update again and finish by saying what you will do next and when you will report back.

expressions.def: going to plan, at the expected point
delayed by something outside your control
meet an unexpected problem
the further result a delay causes elsewhere
likely to fail or be missed
move a date later
contact someone to make something happen
report again later with an answer

see.where: You are in a project meeting.
see.asks: Can you give us a quick update on the project?
see.goal: Answer in about 30 seconds so that everyone in the room knows where things stand and what happens next.

hear.model: The project is progressing well. We're currently delayed by a supplier issue. This may affect Friday's delivery. We're working with the supplier and expect an update tomorrow.
hear.note: Four short sentences. One move each. No preamble.

missions.prompt: Can you give us a quick update on the project?
missions.context: Your team is building a new customer portal. Two of the three stages are finished. The design agency has not sent the final logo files, and the launch is planned for Friday.

see.where: You are at your desk. The warehouse has just called.
see.asks: The supplier delivered the materials late. What does this mean for the project?
see.goal: Nobody is going to prompt you this time. Use the same four moves on a situation you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: The supplier delivered the materials late. What does this mean for the project?
missions.context: The materials arrived three days late. Installation was due to start on Monday. The customer has been promised the site by the end of the month.

competencies.title: Raise a problem
competencies.objective: Explain a problem, what caused it and what it costs, then ask for the decision or the help you actually need.
competencies.pattern: ISSUE → CAUSE → IMPACT → WHAT I'VE DONE → WHAT I NEED

shadow.title: Business English - 925 English Lesson 33 - How to Explain a Problem in English
shadow.why: A lesson on this exact job: state the problem generally, tell the story of what caused it, and ask for help politely. It models three of the five moves — issue, cause and ask — and not impact or what you have already done, so it supports this competency without standing in for it.

moves.label: The problem
moves.hint: Name it in one sentence, before any of the story. A listener who does not know what is wrong cannot follow what happened.
patterns: We've got a problem with the delivery.
There's an issue with the monthly figures.
The machine on line two has stopped.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with one short sentence naming what is wrong — before you explain how it happened.

moves.label: Cause
moves.hint: What actually happened, in the past tense. Be specific about the event, not about whose fault it was.
patterns: It started when the supplier changed our order number.
What happened was the report got switched off in August.
The delay was caused by a late delivery.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what actually happened — one sentence in the past tense, naming the event that started it.
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "because". "I'm raising it because it affects Friday" is an impact sentence, and crediting it as a cause would tell a learner they had explained what happened when they had not.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it costs: the date, the money or the customer. Without this nobody knows how hard to work on it.
patterns: This means installation cannot start on Monday.
We would finish three days late.
It puts the Thursday board pack at risk.
moves.retry: Say it again and say what the problem costs — name the date, the days or the person who feels it.

moves.label: What I've done
moves.hint: The step you have already taken. It is what stops a problem sounding like a complaint.
patterns: I've already spoken to their office.
In the meantime we're using the old report.
We've put a temporary fix in place.
moves.retry: Say it again and add the one thing you have already done about it, before you say what you need.
moves._cue_note: Narrow on purpose, and narrower than it looks. A bare "we've already" fires inside "we've already lost two days", which is an impact statement — it would credit the learner with handling a problem they had only described. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner one retry.

moves.label: What I need
moves.hint: The decision, the person or the permission you want. This is the move almost everyone leaves out, and it is the reason for speaking at all.
patterns: Could you approve the courier cost?
Would you mind chasing them at your level?
What I need from you is a decision on the date.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with a plain question — what do you need this person to decide, approve or do?
cues: what would you like me to

expressions.def: raise something early, before it becomes a surprise
the thing that actually started it, not what you noticed first
cost us time we had already planned to use
fail to finish by the agreed date
a temporary way round a problem while it is being fixed
in the time before it is properly fixed
formally approve something so the work can go ahead
a polite way to ask someone to do something

see.where: You are at your desk. The work has stopped, and your manager is walking past.
see.asks: You look worried — what's going on?
see.goal: Explain it in about 30 seconds, so your manager knows what is wrong, what it costs, and what you need from them.

hear.model: We've got a problem with the delivery. It started when the supplier changed our order number. This means installation cannot start on Monday, so we would finish three days late. I've already spoken to their office and asked them for a new date. Could you approve the courier cost if they can get the parts here on Saturday?
hear.note: Five short sentences. One move each. The ask comes last, and it is a real question.

missions.prompt: You look worried — what's going on?
missions.context: The parts for Monday's installation have not arrived. The supplier changed the order number and the shipment went to the wrong depot. The customer has been promised the site by the end of the month. A Saturday courier would cost extra.

see.where: You are in Monday's team meeting. The problem is not yours — you are just the one who found it.
see.who: The project lead, in front of the team
see.asks: Anything anyone wants to raise before we finish?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time, and the whole team is listening. Use the same five moves on a problem you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: Anything anyone wants to raise before we finish?
missions.context: On Friday you noticed the monthly figures are coming from a report that was switched off in August. Two months of numbers may be wrong. The board pack goes out on Thursday.

competencies.title: Clarifying, asking questions & confirming
competencies.objective: Stop staying silent when something is unclear: say that it is, ask one precise question, say back what you heard, and confirm what happens next.
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The audit's candidate 54ebEjg4EM8 ('Ask Better Questions') is about deepening personal conversation and contains none of this competency's language. The nearest real content is kBlTRXvZlCE ('How to Be Taken Seriously as a New Manager'), which models asking a precise question and 'here's what I'm hearing so far' as leadership signalling, and v60wdYHP4kA ('Building Trust'), which teaches 'let me make sure I understood you — you said…' as active listening. Neither is about clarifying an unclear instruction at work and neither models confirming the next step, so linking one would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. Revisit when the library has a clip on this exact job; a reviewer may choose to link kBlTRXvZlCE.

moves.label: Flag the gap
moves.hint: Say plainly that something is not clear to you yet. One sentence, before any question — a listener who does not know you are lost cannot help you.
patterns: Sorry, one thing isn't clear to me yet.
I'm not sure I follow the timeline.
Just to make sure I understand this properly…
moves.retry: Say it again and open by saying plainly that something is not clear yet — before you ask your question.
cues: make sure i get this right
make sure we're on the same page
make sure we are on the same page
one thing i am not sure
one thing i want to check
one thing i need to check
one thing i'd like to check
one thing i would like to check
i would like to be sure
moves._cue_note: Openers only: the move is admitting the gap, not asking about it. "Just to confirm" and "so to confirm" are deliberately absent everywhere in this competency — spoken before a paraphrase they are a flag, spoken before a plan they are a confirmation, and crediting either move from them would guess.

moves.label: Ask one question
moves.hint: One precise question about the thing you are missing — the date, the person, the scope or the number. "Can you explain?" is not precise.
patterns: When you say soon, do you mean before Friday's review?
Are you asking for the full report or just the summary?
What timeline are we working against?
moves.retry: Say it again and ask one precise question — name the exact thing you need to know: the date, the person, the number or the scope.
cues: could you give me an example
can you give me an example
what does it need to include
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "do you want" or "would you like". "Do you want me to start today?" is a question about the next step, not about the gap — it belongs to confirm if anywhere, and crediting the ask from it would tell a learner they had pinned down the instruction when they had not. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one.

moves.label: Say it back
moves.hint: Repeat the instruction in your own words — what, by when, for whom. It is how the other person hears the gap before it turns into a mistake.
patterns: So you're saying you need the March metrics on the new dashboard, before Friday.
If I've understood correctly, the client wants the quote today and the date can follow.
So the priority is the summary — the full report can wait.
moves.retry: Say it again and say back what you heard, in your own words — what, by when and for whom — before you commit to anything.
cues: if i have got that right
if i have got this right
correct me if i am wrong
moves._cue_note: No bare "is that right" or "is that correct": tagged onto a plan ("I'll send it Friday, is that right?") they close a confirmation, and crediting a paraphrase from them would guess. "Did I get that right?" stays, because it can only follow something said back.

moves.label: Confirm the next step
moves.hint: Close with what happens now — who does what, by when — and get a yes. Without this, nothing was actually agreed.
patterns: So to summarise what we agreed: I'll send the summary by Thursday.
Then I'll start on the March numbers today and check in with you tomorrow — does that work?
Before we move on, can we confirm the review is Wednesday afternoon?
moves.retry: Say it again and finish by confirming the next step — who does what, by when — and ask for a yes.
cues: i will come back to you
i will get back to you
moves._cue_note: A confirmation is a commitment ("then I'll…") or an explicit agreement check ("can we confirm…", "does that work?"). A deadline on its own ("by Friday") is not one — it belongs just as naturally inside a paraphrase — so no day or date is a cue here.

expressions.w: just to make sure I understand
expressions.def: a polite way to say you are about to check something before you act
a short, polite way to say you have lost the thread
ask someone to say exactly what a word or phrase covers
explain something step by step, from the start
the words that begin a paraphrase of what you just heard
the same idea again, said more simply
the decision both sides have accepted
a pause to lock something in before the next topic

see.where: You are in the Monday planning meeting. Your manager has just handed you a task and is already moving on to the next point.
see.asks: We need the new dashboard done soon — the usual metrics, same as last time. Can you take that?
see.goal: Don't just say yes. In about 30 seconds: say what is unclear, ask one precise question, say back what you heard, and confirm what you will do next.

hear.model: Sorry, one thing isn't clear to me yet. When you say soon, do you mean before Friday's review or by the end of the month? So you're saying the same six metrics as March, on the new dashboard. Then I'll build it with those six and have a first version to you by Thursday — does that work?
hear.note: Four moves, one each. The question names the exact gap — "soon". The last line is a plan and a request for a yes.

missions.prompt: We need the new dashboard done soon — the usual metrics, same as last time. Can you take that?
missions.context: "Soon" has not been defined: the quarterly review is on Friday and the board pack goes out at the end of the month. "The usual metrics" were the six numbers on the March dashboard — the sales team has since asked for two more. You could have a first version ready by Thursday.

see.where: A colleague from the client team calls you between meetings. She is in a hurry, and the line is not great.
see.who: A colleague from the client team, on the phone
see.asks: Can you sort out the client thing before the review? They're expecting it.
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Before you agree to anything, use the same four moves on an instruction you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: Can you sort out the client thing before the review? They're expecting it.
missions.context: There are two open items for this client: a revised quote, and the delivery date they asked about last week. The review is on Wednesday afternoon. You can send the quote today; the delivery date needs an answer from the warehouse, which usually replies within a day.
